en: The *Tathāgatajñānamudrā-sūtra*, one fascicle.
Sengyou states that the translator is unknown; it is now appended to the Song Records.
Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove, together with...

There was a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, along with thirty trillion bodhisattvas, all of whom had attained dhāraṇīs and dwelt in the unattached dharma-gate of the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; they had attained the gate of dhāraṇīs, knew whether the faculties of all sentient beings were complete or incomplete, and further knew all the conduct of sentient beings.

At that time, the World-Honored One entered the Samādhi of the Buddha’s Domain, which is without form, without grasping, without demonstration, without shape, without designation, without root, without change, without attainment, without self, without master, without action, without non-action, without coming, without going, without abiding, without objective support, unconditioned, neither conditioned nor non-conditioned, not associated, not dissociated, without mind, not the activity of mind, not real, not unreal, not present, not near, and not separated from all dharmas.

When entering this samādhi, one does not see the body of the Tathāgata nor the marks of his body; one does not see the mind nor the marks of the mind; one does not see the robes, nor the seat, nor that upon which he sits, nor his walking.

This samādhi gives rise to all manner of meritorious qualities; it is the realm of the Buddhas. From within this very concentration, he emits a great light that shines everywhere throughout the trichiliocosm. Within this world-system, the light of the sun, moon, and stars; the brilliance of wondrous jewels and divine pearls; the glow of fire and lightning; and even the radiance of the celestial palaces of Śakra and up to those of Brahmā—all these are completely eclipsed and no longer appear.
By the power of the Tathāgata’s samādhi, the myriad exquisite fragrances are heard throughout the trichiliocosm; among all the devas, none can perceive the fragrance of his light.
In all places of darkness and obscurity between worlds, the Buddha’s light shines universally, such that there is nowhere it does not illuminate with great brilliance.
Mount Cakravāḍa, Mount Mahācakravāḍa, Sumeru the king of mountains, and all other famous mountains—the sentient beings therein do not perceive their original forms.
At that time, a net of the seven treasures covered the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system, manifesting a rare and marvelous sign;
in all worlds, wondrous and extraordinary flowers blossomed.
The Kalandaka Bamboo Grove and Vulture Peak Mountain were joined together as a single assembly; the ground was level and smooth, and there grew thousand-petaled lotuses as large as chariot wheels.
Upon each flower was a canopy of seven-jeweled nets, exquisitely adorned and magnificent, draped and spread out like clouds.
The realm of Magadha was entirely soft and supple, like a garment of kālinga cloth.

At that time, the Buddhas of worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the eastern direction addressed ten thousand asaṃkhyeya bodhisattvas, all of whom were in their final birth before buddhahood:
"Go to the Sahā world."
In that land there is a Buddha named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who shall preach the samādhi called "The Seal of Tathāgata Wisdom" for entering the realm of all Buddhas.
The Buddha has now entered this samādhi.
If there is a bodhisattva who hears of this samādhi, it is superior to practicing the six pāramitās for hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
You should go and listen.

Those bodhisattvas, each by means of their own supernormal power, reached the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in the Sahā world in the time it takes to bend and extend one’s arm. They approached the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him seven times, and sat upon lotus thrones.
The same was true for the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.

At that time, all the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and those who had resolved upon the Great Mind within this trichiliocosm gathered together; they proceeded to the Bamboo Grove and arrived at the place where the Buddha was.
Furthermore, in this world, eight billion bodhisattvas gathered together in a single moment and took their seats in order among the fourfold assembly.
Furthermore, there were three hundred thousand śrāvakas who had received the Buddha’s meditative concentration, all present in the assembly.

From Śakra-devendra and the four world-protecting kings of this trichiliocosm, up to Maheśvara, the Śuddhāvāsa devas, and so forth—including all dragon kings, yakṣa kings, gandharva kings, garuḍa kings, and asura kings—each surrounded by countless retinues, came to the assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and took their seats in order.
At that time, the assemblies of great majesty and virtue in this trichiliocosm all gathered like clouds, reaching as far as the Brahma world without any empty space remaining.
Then Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Mahākauṣṭhila, Mahākātyāyana, Subhūti, and Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked Mañjuśrī, "Where is the Tathāgata now?"
"By what form and appearance is the Tathāgata seen?
What are the characteristics of the Tathāgata’s focused mindfulness?
Mañjuśrī replied:

“You śrāvakas have achieved great wisdom and mastery over samādhi; each of you should, by means of your power of concentration, observe the Buddha’s body and the locus of your focused mindfulness to see where they abide.”
The great śrāvakas entered into samādhi and contemplated, yet they could not see the Buddha’s body nor the place where his mindfulness was fixed.
At that time, the śrāvakas searched and investigated throughout this trichiliocosm, but they could neither see the Buddha’s body nor perceive any marks of his physical form.
“In this way, Mañjuśrī,
one does not see the Tathāgata nor the focal point for mindfulness.
How then can I now perceive the body of the Buddha?”
Mañjuśrī replied,
“Wait but a moment, and you shall see the Buddha yourself.
At that time, the World-Honored One arose from samādhi, and the trichiliocosm immediately shook with great intensity.
The Buddha’s body was extraordinary, its majestic radiance shining brilliantly.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
What are the characteristics of the samādhi into which the Tathāgata enters?
Even when the great śrāvakas observe with their wisdom-eye, they are entirely unable to see it.
What is the objective realm of this samādhi?
At that time, the Buddha told Śāriputra:
"This samādhi is without object and without location; it is the realm of the Buddhas, not something known by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas."
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
The realm of the Tathāgata is inconceivable; this is the supernatural power of the Buddha. Śāriputra!
The Buddha-body is real, yet it is no-body; it is not made, not arisen, not extinguished, nor is it nurtured;
it is not a transformation, not an object of faith, quiescent, unconditioned, traceless, without activity, without "this," and without "that";
its intrinsic nature is pure, there is not a single dharma within it, and it is neither receiving nor—
It is not a wish, not born, not a result of retribution, not seen, not heard, not perceived, not designated,
not smelled, not tasted, not touched, not afflicted, not deliberated, not opposed, not mind,
not recollection, not thought, not non-thought, not entering, not coming, not...
It is gone; it is the severance of the path of going and coming;

it is not a shadow, not a flaw, not a cessation, not a thing, not real, not made, not created, not accomplished, not grasped, not concealed, not manifest, not dependent, not darkness, not light; it is quiescent, yet not quiescent; it is eternally abiding.
Tranquil concentration, purity, impurity, natural purity; the non-existence of any dharma; that which is neither born nor arisen;
neither craving nor dwelling in stillness; neither a location nor movement;
neither affliction nor speech; neither dharma nor non-dharma; neither a field of merit nor not a field of merit; and non-extinction.
It is not non-exhaustion; it is the relinquishing of all attachments, which is called emptiness. It is not conflict; it is without sound; it is free from names and words;
it relinquishes recollection and conceptualization. It is neither associated nor dissociated; it is neither cessation nor non-cessation;
it is neither measurable nor immeasurable; it is neither going nor returning; it is not dual.
It is not duality, not this shore, not the other shore, not the middle stream;
it is not partial, not non-partial; it is not karma, not retribution; it is not hearing, not thinking, not measuring;
it is not an obstruction, not a characteristic, not non-characteristic; it is not a gate, not detachment, not attachment—it is the practice of bliss.
All dharmas share the same characteristic as dharmas: they are suchness and reality. For the sake of delivering sentient beings, yet in truth there are none to be delivered;
they liberate those not yet liberated, discipline those not yet disciplined, and rescue those not yet rescued.
They demonstrate the dharma of non-demonstration—neither equal nor unequal, neither similar nor dissimilar, and without equality.
Amṛta and the like; equality with emptiness; the state of non-abiding; non-attainment and the like;
cessation; total extinction; the sphere of well-tamed conduct; the turning of the non-retrogressive wheel; certainty free from doubt;
neither distinct nor separate; the non-dual dharma; the purity of what is practiced; fundamental conduct; and the endowment of majestic deportment and liberation.
The feet are neither long nor short, neither square nor round;

they are not the marks of the body, not the marks of the aggregates (*skandha*), not the marks of the sense bases (*āyatana*), and not the marks of the elements (*dhātu*). They do not arise from the conditioned, nor do they arise from the unconditioned;
they are not the reality of the unconditioned. They are not life, nor are they non-life; they are not birth, nor are they manifestation; they are non-existent.
It is not a vision; it is not truly born, not expressible in words, not an object of intellectual acceptance; its bodily marks are immovable;
it is not inverted, not wavering, not real, not recollectable, not a composite, not an action, not a non-action, not luminous, not a characteristic, not nirvāṇa, not entering nirvāṇa, and not fixed.
“...nor is it non-non-concentration.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“This is called the bodily mark of the Tathāgata.”
"All sentient beings rely upon signs; is there anyone who can know this samādhi?
"Certainly, World-Honored One!
Within all signs, the Buddha-body cannot be found."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to expand the Tathāgata’s Samādhi of the Seal of Wisdom, spoke these verses:
“The body is not a body, for it is liberated from the body; It is without action, without destruction, and without attainment.
Phenomena are neither associated nor dissociated; This is what is revealed as the body of the Sugata.”
Neither joined nor unjoined, it is free from defilement and attachment; neither grasping nor abandoning, neither equal nor long;
neither created, nor a locus, nor a non-locus—this body is not manifest and has no desires.
Neither grasped nor created, it is non-existent; Neither form nor mind, neither dual nor single;
Without parts, without division, without arising or ceasing— This true reality, devoid of self, manifests as the Buddha-body.
Neither strong nor weak, nor is it annihilation; Neither silence, nor aspiration, nor the exhaustion of offerings;
Neither attainment, nor meditative concentration, nor a point of reliance— The true body manifests thus, free from all defilement.
Neither seen nor heard, neither smelled nor touched, Not based on designations, yet manifesting as reflections;
If there are those who see this, their hearts rejoice, And thus they achieve the preaching of the Dharma.
Neither aggregates, nor elements, nor reality or unreality; The sense faculties are neither born, nor defiled, nor pure;
Neither solid nor non-solid, appearing like the moon in water— Thus one should contemplate the body of the Sugata.
Arising from causes and conditions, it is not real; Neither arising nor ceasing, neither moving nor departing;
Not manifesting yet manifesting the three [bodies] like a magician— Contemplating the Buddha in this way, one has no basis for reliance.
Neither tranquil nor non-tranquil, neither associated; Neither bound, nor desirous, nor joined, nor dispersed.
Like an empty fist, its interior is truly void; To contemplate thus is the true offering to the Buddha.
If one were to gather precious jewels from billions of lands throughout the worlds of the ten directions, filling them as high as the Brahma realm,
and offer them to all Buddhas for immeasurable eons— the merit of one who transcribes this [sutra] would surpass that.
Even if one were to practice the four immeasurables throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges for eons beyond measure,
and maintain pure precepts incomparable to any other, the merit of believing and understanding this sutra is most supreme.
From beginningless saṃsāra until this present body, one has practiced patience toward all sentient beings;
yet if there were someone who briefly believed in the *Jñānamudrā-sūtra*, that person would be like a grain of mustard seed compared to Mount Sumeru.
If one were to carry all the various kinds of sentient beings in the three realms upon the crown of one’s head for immeasurable eons—
without physical fatigue or weariness and without regret— the merit of being able to endure this sutra would be beyond compare.
If beings as numerous as the sands of a hundred worlds were to practice meditative concentration for immeasurable eons,
the merit of holding this sutra for a single day and night would surpass theirs beyond measure.
The wise abandon the two extremes and practice the Middle Way;
though they have passed through kalpas as numerous as infinite atoms, if one understands this sutra according to its teaching, that [merit] is but a single drop in the great ocean.
One should not contemplate the Buddha through the marks of physical form; do not examine the Buddha as a fool would.
Subhūti, he who sees my true nature is the most pure field of merit within the three realms.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:
“This is the Tathāgata-jñāna-mudrā-samādhi, which is fully able to satisfy the unobstructed wisdom of all bodhisattvas in all worlds throughout the ten directions.”
Śāriputra! If you wish to see quickly all the Buddhas and bodhisattvas of the ten directions, practice this samādhi with diligent effort day and night, and you shall see them all.
Śāriputra! This samādhi is the bodhisattva’s gateway of immeasurable doors, a dhāraṇī that pervades all practices; it can sustain the dharma-realm so that it remains uninterrupted.

This dhāraṇī upholds all dharma-gates; if one accomplishes these characteristics, they are called a bodhisattva. They are able to achieve the thirty-two marks and eighty minor signs, possess corresponding practices, and have pure karmic conduct. They transcend the realm of Māra, remaining unmoving and non-emergent, practicing the conduct of a Buddha equally, with the actions of body, speech, and mind all being completely purified.
Those who wish to understand the Tathāgata’s secret Dharma should practice and study this samādhi;
those who wish to preach the Dharma in successive order should also study this samādhi;

those who wish to know all phenomena exhaustively, those who wish to know the ultimate truth, those who wish to realize the proof of billions of births and deaths, those who wish to understand the twelve links of dependent origination, those who wish to understand the intentions and conducts of all sentient beings, and those who wish to attain a pure and wondrous Buddha-land, should study this samādhi.

Those who wish to obtain sublime radiance, wish to bring about the accomplishment of a retinue, wish to act as a refuge for sentient beings, wish to accomplish the primary and secondary marks, wish to accomplish the eloquence of joyful speech, and wish to know all dharmas, should study this samādhi.
Why is this? Śāriputra,
it is because they are like wish-fulfilling jewels (cintāmaṇi), which fulfill all desires according to the wishes of sentient beings.
In this way, Śāriputra, this samādhi is the source of all sublime matters for bodhisattvas; it is fully capable of fulfilling all vows and practices.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Supreme wisdom, the light of the highest intelligence; The light of wisdom, the wealth of wisdom, the treasury of the wealth of wisdom;
That which is wrought by wisdom, entering the gateway of wisdom— The seal of immeasurable wisdom seals this sutra."
The faculty of wisdom takes knowledge as its ground for wisdom; Knowledge arises, and the light of knowledge extinguishes all darkness.
Wisdom is inexhaustible, and wisdom reveals; Like the sun and moon among the various sūtras, it illuminates the three realms.
The samādhis of equality, impartiality, and so forth, Which sever all fetters through the true nature of phenomena;
The gateway to the wisdom-seal of all samādhis— This is the Buddha-lineage’s fourfold wondrous eloquence.

Extinguishing defilements without end, crossing to the further shore; A treasury of virtue, arising of merit, universally responding with blessings— This is the root of the happiness I have attained; This samādhi is the treasure of the Sugata.
Just as a king who loves his country and skillfully governs his people receives abundant, supreme, and wondrous treasures according to their needs,
so too does this Ocean of Jewels now preach this sutra to wash away greed, hatred, and delusion.
Skillful tranquility can extinguish [defilements] through mindfulness; skillfully removing all impurities, it purifies the view of self.
Like a strong man wielding a sword to destroy what cannot be destroyed, the Buddha’s retribution grants this seal of dhāraṇī.
Intelligence protects and shelters all sentient beings; through the deeds of wisdom, one becomes richly endowed with it.
The light of wisdom shines universally without limit; by means of this sutra, one shall attain the gateway of wisdom.
Having severed the two perceptions of disciplining oneself and disciplining others, and having extinguished the sixty-two views, cravings, and the like,
one enters the Tathāgata’s gate of ambrosia and shall attain the thirty-two marks of excellence.
The path, the supreme path, and the sequential path; the factors conducive to enlightenment and those that are not;
he is well able to awaken the indolent—such are the immeasurable and inexhaustible characteristics of his wisdom.
Through sequential understanding in accordance with the Dharma, The dharani of immeasurable light of wisdom is attained;
The perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā) is thereby accomplished, And the same applies to ethical discipline (śīla) and patience (kṣānti);
Vigor (vīrya), meditation (dhyāna), and wisdom (prajñā) are inexhaustible— Abiding in this wisdom, one accomplishes the perfections.
Do not fear the retribution of karma or afflictions, nor fear the hosts of Māras or the evil realms;
by practicing and gathering this sutra without hindrance, one shall attain the Way according to one's aspirations.
All you sons of the Buddhas dwelling within this Bhadrakalpa, who have gathered from the ten directions to bear witness for me—
since those whose dharma-vessels are indestructible have all assembled here, you should all uphold the teachings of this sutra.
This sutra can give birth to the Buddhas of the past, And is likewise the mother of all Buddhas of the future;
It can also give birth to the Buddhas of the present— Those who diligently cultivate this sutra are brothers to the Buddhas.
With karma purified and conduct stainless, one’s practice never regresses; transcending the mire, one ascends to the immovable.
Those who respond to this sutra abide in reality and shall attain the Tathāgata’s wondrous treasury of Dharma.

At that time, as the World-Honored One extensively expounded this Dharma, thirty bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, attained this samādhi; and sixty-eight billion nayutas of bodhisattvas, who had already purified their various practices over hundreds of thousands of kalpas, attained non-retrogression from the unsurpassed path, as well as the *Dhāraṇī of the Exhaustless Sound and Wisdom-Light*.

Furthermore, there were six hundred thousand devas and humans who had not yet resolved to attain unexcelled bodhicitta; they all now gave rise to that intention, and upon hearing this samādhi, they all felt sympathetic joy.
At the moment he gave rise to sympathetic joy, he immediately attained the stage of *avaivartika*.
The Buddha conferred upon him a prediction, saying that after thirty thousand *kalpas* in a future age, he would attain Buddhahood and be named Fearless (*Abhaya*).

Furthermore, there were those who had long practiced and attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), each attaining the Unsurpassed Way in different lands, all bearing the same name.
At that time, the World-Honored One, surrounded by the fourfold assembly, addressed Mañjuśrī:

"You who abide in the dharma of non-abiding, who do not engage in conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and do not perform conditioned activities—since all dharmas have no basis—you should protect this Unsurpassed Way and expound it widely for the sake of others."
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I observe that all dharmas are unobtainable.”

I shall protect this unsurpassed enlightenment, just as the World-Honored One’s unsurpassed path is without abiding, without non-abiding, without location, unmanifest, ungraspable, unattainable, and without loss.
At that time, thirty billion bodhisattvas in the assembly rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, joined their palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

We, too, wish to protect the Dharma of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—which is difficult to attain—cultivated by the Tathāgata over immeasurable, incalculable, and nayuta-kalpas.
Each of them removed the upper garment they were wearing and offered it to the Tathāgata, making the supreme vow.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva:
“You should listen attentively!”
"Maitreya, you should know that this is your task!
In the future age, during the final five hundred years, you shall protect this sutra!
Maitreya addressed the Buddha:
“Yes, World-Honored One!
I shall protect it!
The Buddha said to Maitreya:
"Among these thirty billion bodhisattvas, eight thousand bodhisattvas shall protect and uphold the True Dharma.

The remaining bodhisattvas have not yet mastered self-discipline and do not protect the True Dharma; in the future final age, amidst this True Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—which was difficult to attain and was cultivated and accumulated by the Tathāgata over incalculable eons—they will give rise to disputes, disparage it and fail to speak of it, they will be unable to listen to or receive it, and they will be unable to protect or uphold it."
“Maitreya! There are seven dharmas that give rise to the bodhicitta.
What are these seven?
First, generating the bodhicitta as the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have done.
Second, generating the bodhicitta for the sake of protecting and upholding the True Dharma when it is about to perish.
Third, seeing all sentient beings oppressed by manifold sufferings, they give rise to great compassion and resolve their minds on bodhicitta.
Fourth, Bodhisattvas teach other sentient beings to resolve their minds on bodhicitta.
Fifth, when practicing giving, one personally generates the bodhicitta.
Sixth, seeing others resolve their minds [for enlightenment], one follows their example and generates the mind.
Seventh, seeing the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, fully adorned and magnificent, or hearing of them, one generates the mind.
Maitreya! Thus, through these seven causes and conditions, one generates the bodhicitta,
just as the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas generate the bodhicitta.
When the True Dharma is about to perish, one generates the bodhicitta for the sake of its protection and preservation;
seeing all sentient beings oppressed by manifold sufferings, one gives rise to great compassion and generates the bodhicitta.

By generating these three types of mind, one is able to protect and preserve the True Dharma for all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and can also swiftly attain the stage of non-retrogression and accomplish the Buddha-way.
The latter four types of resolve are stubborn and difficult to subdue; they are unable to protect the Dharma.
"Furthermore, Maitreya!
When a bodhisattva accomplishes five dharmas, he should be thus considered non-retrogressive (avaivartika)."
What are these five?
First, to give rise to a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings.
Second, to feel no jealousy when seeing others obtain benefit.
Third, upon seeing those who protect the Dharma, one would rather lose one's own body and life than speak of their faults.
Fourth, one is able to relinquish all gain and offerings.
Fifth, one has faith in the profound Dharma and does not believe in worldly scriptures, prose, or verse.
"Maitreya!
When a bodhisattva accomplishes these five dharmas, they are called 'non-retrogressive.
Furthermore, Maitreya!"
Furthermore, there are five qualities of a bodhisattva whose mind is rigid and harsh, which can destroy the True Dharma.
What are these five?
First, giving rise to unwholesome physical form.
Second, they place their trust in base conduct.
Third, they are greedily attached to gain and offerings.
Fourth, they cherish and protect their donors.
Fifth, harboring a mind of flattery and crookedness, one’s conduct is not genuine; though one speaks of emptiness with the mouth, one’s actions do not correspond to it.
These are the five things that destroy the True Dharma.
"Furthermore, Maitreya,
there are five more dharmas by which a bodhisattva achieves the state of *avaivartika*.
What are these five?
First, one does not apprehend a self;
second, one does not apprehend sentient beings;
third, one thoroughly realizes that the dharma-realm is without apprehension and without expression.
Fourth, they do not attain bodhi.
Fifth, they do not perceive the Tathāgata by means of the physical body.
Maitreya!
“When a bodhisattva accomplishes these five dharmas, they are called an avaivartika.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“Giving rise to jealousy out of wisdom is like a wood-worm destroying timber;”
Not relying on verbal faith or base views, one can protect the Buddha’s bodhi.
Cultivating diligence in the wilderness, with deep patience and constant silence,
like a rhinoceros separated from its herd, one skillfully guards the Path so it is not lost.
Staying far from the multitude and delighting in solitude, like a startled deer longing for stillness;
unattached like the wind in the sky—such conduct can uphold the Dharma.
Not begrudging body or life, and remaining unstained by affection for kin, [one dwells in the forest].
Diligently cultivating emptiness and non-self, one is able to achieve bodhi.
In future generations there will be sentient beings who say, "I practice for bodhi," yet their minds are fickle, deceitful, and crooked; they cannot protect the true Dharma.
I recall that before the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, more than eighty billion kalpas ago,
there was a Buddha named Candracūḍa who expounded this samādhi.
In his first assembly, there were eighty billion nayutas of bodhisattvas.
Hearing the Buddha expound the Dharma, all attained the stage of non-retrogression.
At the second assembly where he preached the Dharma, there were seventy-three *yojana*;
at the third assembly where they heard the Dharma, there were seven billion *yojana*.
The Buddha’s lifespan was immeasurable kalpas; his radiance extended for sixty yojanas;
his assembly numbered nine hundred and ninety million; they were free from birth and possessed mastery of mind.
At that time, there was a wheel-turning king named Huiqi (Wisdom-Arising).
The king ruled over Jambudvīpa, seventy thousand yojanas in extent,
as well as the four continents; he had sixty billion court ladies and a thousand sons, and his residence was named Radiant Joy.
A hundred thousand cities were adorned, with gardens and pavilions all fully provided;
they were all prosperous, joyful, and flourishing, just like the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
In his dream, the king heard a voice proclaiming that the Buddha Candracūḍa had appeared in the world.
One hundred and sixty billion beings together proceeded before the Buddha.
At that time, the king, having heard this sutra on the profound meditative concentration of the Dharma-body,
immediately relinquished his kingdom to serve the Buddha, praying only that it be used as [the Buddha] saw fit.
In every city he erected vihāras, all made of exquisite sandalwood;
he further provided numerous servants and attendants, and spread gold upon the grounds for walking meditation.
Thus the King made offerings to the Buddha for a full eighty thousand years.
Dedicated and focused, he neither slept nor lay down;
without weariness or stinginess, he provided offerings every day in immeasurable numbers.
All these offerings were bestowed upon the Buddha for the sake of seeking this samādhi.
Dwelling in seclusion, he cultivated tranquil mindfulness; the samādhi was most profound and wondrous.
It is not attained through signs, nor is it gained by clever expedients.
He immediately abandoned his kingdom and went forth into homelessness, donning the robes of Śāṇa.
For three thousand years he maintained focused mindfulness, contemplating meditative concentration without reclining or lying down.
During that interval, the Buddha preached the Dharma to bring about understanding;
after his parinirvāṇa, sixty-four trillion stūpas were erected.
Each was given five hundred parasols, adorned with the seven treasures;
each had a hundred musical performances and was illuminated by eight thousand lamps.
Clad in coarse, soiled garments, they remained thus for seventy-three thousand years.
They constantly preach this samādhi and praise being free from attachment; they do not seek worldly superior knowledge,
they beg for alms and do not accept invitations, and they dwell in reliance upon the protection of the Dharma.
If one were to offer all the pure precepts upheld by eighty trillion nayutas of Buddhas as the aforementioned offerings, one would fully possess this samādhi.
If you wish to attain bodhi, you should learn in the manner of the Buddha.
Do not trust those who discourse on unorthodox paths; instead, reverently cultivate this sutra.

Those who speak of practicing the Way in future lives yet turn back to destroy the prohibitions and precepts, acting for profit rather than for the Dharma—though they read it, they do not understand emptiness.
He preached emptiness but did not understand it; his livelihood was wrong and he was impure.
Though he discoursed on emptiness, he grasped at emptiness, yet claimed himself that he had no doubts regarding the Way.
At that time, King Huiqi was none other than Amitābha Buddha.
Those who were the king’s thousand sons at that time are now the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa.
Those who at that time left the household life together with the king, along with their retinues and disciples,
are now these fourfold assemblies gathered before me.
Minding billions of nayutas of Buddhas, he left the home life and heard the True Dharma;
upon hearing it, he was able to receive and uphold it, attaining emptiness and non-reliance.
He gave rise to immeasurable skillful means to make offerings to all Tathāgatas.
Not perceiving the marks of bodhi is entirely due to practicing the truth.
Having seen Dīpaṃkara Buddha, he severed his seeking and attained equanimity;
at that moment, he was granted the prediction: "In the future, you shall become a Buddha."
At that time, there was a woman named Bhadrottamā—the chief queen of King Bimbisāra—and another lady named Suvarṇaprabhāsā, the daughter of Kuntī;

they rose from their seats and approached the Buddha. Each took five hundred bundles of seven-jeweled flowers, placed them in the folds of their robes, and scattered them over the Buddha. They also offered to the Tathāgata karpāsa garments worth hundreds of thousands and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
I have faith in, understand, and uphold this samādhi.
To those who recite it, I shall provide protection and supply whatever they require according to their needs and desires.

I shall teach and transform sentient beings by means of the Mahāyāna Dharma, without saying that this is empty or that this is not empty; I shall not merely engage in verbal discourse, but will resolutely uphold [the teaching] and practice exactly as it is taught, not sparing even my own body or life, let alone wealth or treasures!
"You should also act as instructed, teaching one another in succession.

At that time, eight thousand women from King Bimbisāra’s inner palace and sixty thousand upāsikās from the kingdom of Magadha all resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta; they expressed their sympathetic joy toward this samādhi and made this vow:
"In the future final age, we shall protect the True Dharma!"
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing their thoughts, immediately smiled.
Wondrous rays of light of various colors issued from his mouth, illuminating the ten directions universally, and then returned to enter through the crown of his head.
At that time, Bhadramukha, born of golden light, conceived a heart of faith and reverence; he then spoke together with a single voice in verse:
"The Victorious One is a mass of virtues peerless as a Buddha, A tree of merit-flowers, the King among stars.
Your speech is gentle, gladdening, and sweet in its sequence— For what reason, World-Honored One of Ten Powers, do you smile?"
Your face is round like the moon, opening the eyes of the world; your Brahma-voice is pure and universally delights those who hear it.
You tame the fierce and soften the stiff, gladdening body and mind—O Lion among Men, for what reason do you smile?
Harmonious, patient, and free from turbidity, your speech is authentic; Your voice is perfect and endowed with all flavors.
Clearly understanding the immeasurable meanings of all conditioned phenomena, I pray that you, O Mass of Merit, manifest your smile.
Fully endowed with the eight kinds of sublime tones, With sixty qualities of graceful and harmonious sound;
Understanding seven hundred kinds of languages, And penetrating sixty billion meanings and flavors;
Possessing eighty billion corresponding sounds, And likewise ten nayutas of such voices.
O Immeasurable One of Infinite Honor, we pray that you will explain the cause and conditions of your smile.
Most immovable among all mountains, you who understand the meaning of correspondence and extinguish all doubts;
you who can sever all suffering and bring about peace and happiness—O Treasure-Heap, please speak truly of the reason for your smile.
The Golden Mountain explains the vehicle of the seven treasures; Like the flower-moon, he is the delight of all;
Walking alone with a voice like a lion’s, I pray you will explain the cause of your radiance and smile.
Most honored in the three realms, you have purified the three defilements; Through immeasurable eons, you have practiced sublime tranquility.
The light of your smile fills the worlds of the ten directions, Skillfully benefiting beings as you proclaim the gate of ambrosia.
The sounds of zithers, lutes, bronze cymbals, flutes, and pipes; the beating of drums and the blowing of conch shells—these myriad exquisite tones;
the voices of kinnaras and kalaviṅkas; the cries of the sorrowful pheasant, the wild goose, and the *kuci-luo* bird;
and the resonance of the *pi* drum, the cymbals, and the *konghou* lute—all these together cannot equal even a single sublime sound of the Tathāgata.
Thus, the assembly gathered from the ten directions, with their various views each differing;
may you speak truthfully of the extinction of views and craving, so that upon returning to your own land, the vows of the multitude shall be fulfilled.
From each of the ten directions, one hundred million beings have been sent, all gathering here for the sake of the True Dharma;
since you smile, you will surely rain down the rain of Dharma—what teaching will you proclaim to bring joy?
After the virtuous Kāñcanaprabha had spoken these verses, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
"I recall a past eon as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, When there was a Buddha named Puṇyaprabha, the Knower of the World;
His lifespan lasted seven hundred and sixty trillion years, And the number of his śrāvaka assembly was immeasurable."
There was a wheel-turning king named Huiyu (Wisdom-Ruler), whose queen was named Yueguan (Moon-Contemplation) and her successor Yan (Flame).
Renouncing worldly attachment, they sought the True Dharma and constantly upheld it for one hundred million years.
Six hundred trillion and three million [Buddhas], as well as thirty Ganges-sands of future Buddhas,
shall protect the True Dharma here, upholding it so that it is never severed.
At that time, you shall all be born together with King Huiyu, the Buddha Akṣobhya;
by virtue of protecting the Dharma, you shall cast off your female bodies and be reborn in the immeasurable Land of Ultimate Bliss.
This protector of the Dharma shall likewise be born; when the Dharma is about to perish, he shall abide for its sake.
He will surely be born upon a thousand-petaled lotus in Sukhāvatī, adorned with the marks and signs as a son of the Buddha.
Having been born there to make offerings to the Perfectly Awakened Ones, in the adorned King Kalpa free from thorns,
one shall attain the Unsurpassed Way there, upholding the True Dharma for gods and humans.
In that Buddha-land there are no demonic activities; there is no retribution for evil karma, nor is there birth from a womb.
Every day immeasurable bodhisattvas assemble there, and even the names "śrāvaka" and "pratyekabuddha" do not exist.
Sparing neither body nor life to protect the Buddha-way, Not regressing for the sake of fame or reputation,
To swiftly accomplish the Unsurpassed Way, And further desiring to quickly bring all lands to fulfillment.
"You all should harmonize and have faith and reverence for the Buddha; with respectful devotion, protect the Bodhi that has no other refuge.
In this final age when the Great Dharma is about to perish, you must not follow those who crave gain and offerings."
For billions of eons I have given away my wives and children, and sacrificed my head, eyes, and body in pursuit of the Buddha-way;
yet for the sake of profit, I have preached the Dharma improperly, being stingy with donors and giving rise to anger and envy.
Eighty trillion people rose up with tears of compassion; they shall protect the Dharma at its extinction by relying on Bodhi.
The trichiliocosm shook and the heavens rained down flowers; those who love and revere this sutra possess the most excellent lifespan.
If one were to fill Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges with gold and offer it as a gift for immeasurable eons,
even such an offering of Ganges-sands of jewels could not compare to being able to believe in this Sūtra of the Seal of Wisdom.
Do not recklessly bestow this upon those who do not delight in the Way; Upon hearing of the Buddha’s rarity, one should give rise to the mind of the Way.
One should study this sutra in successive order, And practicing according to what is taught, one shall realize Bodhi.
Maintaining precepts and practicing reverence in the wilderness, regarding the assembly as one's own kin through the three karmas,
cultivating the six points of harmonious respect while conceiving the thought of the Buddha— one who seeks the sublime Dharma should study this sutra.
If there are those who transcribe this Dharma-seal, Recite, proclaim, and explain it for others, The merit of their bodies is inconceivable;
These children of the Buddha shall be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How many bodhisattvas will there be in the future who receive and uphold this samādhi?”
The Buddha told Maitreya:
"In future ages, those with faith and joy will be few, while many will destroy their roots of goodness and sever the True Dharma.
To practice this Dharma is extremely difficult, extremely difficult!"
The Buddha told Maitreya:
"If I were to fully describe all the non-concordant practices of future bodhisattvas, they could not be exhausted.
Maitreya addressed the Buddha:
"We pray that you will speak of it!
We pray that you will speak of it!
Out of compassion for us."
"In future ages, there may be those who practice the path of truth; if they hear this sutra and practice according to what is taught, they shall attain the Unsurpassed Way.
The Buddha told Maitreya:
"It is as you have said."

Maitreya, if there are bodhisattvas who have already resolved their minds on enlightenment under a hundred buddhas and planted various roots of goodness, yet in a future life they forget that mind of the Way;
Maitreya!

Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who have resolved their minds upon unsurpassed awakening in the presence of a thousand Buddhas and have planted various roots of goodness; yet, in a future life, they give rise to the thought of awakening but do not believe in the Mahāyāna, and they treat the Mahāyāna with contempt and derision.
Maitreya!

Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who have resolved their minds on enlightenment in the presence of ten thousand Buddhas and planted various roots of goodness; yet in a future age, although they give rise to the bodhicitta and place great faith in the Mahāyāna, they neither uphold nor recite it.
Maitreya!

Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who have resolved their minds on enlightenment in the presence of billions of buddhas and have planted various roots of goodness; yet, when they give rise to the mind of enlightenment in a future life, they may be able to hear and write [the teachings], but they do not understand the profound meaning and cannot reach a definitive certainty.
Maitreya!

Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who, in the presence of ten billion buddhas, have resolved their minds on enlightenment and planted various roots of goodness; yet in a future age, although they give rise to the mind of enlightenment, listen to and receive the Mahāyāna, copy it, and recite it, they do not achieve perfection in patience regarding enlightenment.
Maitreya!

Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who, having awakened the mind of enlightenment under thirty billion buddhas and planted various roots of goodness, will give rise to the mind of enlightenment in a future age; they are able to hear, receive, transcribe, and recite the Mahāyāna upon hearing it, and they have accomplished great patience, yet they are not yet in accord with this samādhi and do not attain the eloquence of correspondence.

"Maitreya! Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who have resolved upon the mind of enlightenment under eighty billion buddhas and have planted various roots of goodness. In a future age, they will give rise to the mind of enlightenment; hearing the Mahāyāna, they are able to receive it, uphold it, transcribe it, and recite it. They shall attain this samādhi, fulfill the power of patience, understand all dharmas, and extensively expound upon bodhi. Māras cannot destroy them, and they shall be free from all karmic obstructions. Any evil deeds committed over incalculable kalpas—such as burning heads, mental affliction, being slandered by others, being mocked, or being ridiculed—shall be eliminated in this very life. They shall reverently make offerings to immeasurable and innumerable buddhas, never regressing from the mind of enlightenment, attaining a firm resolve, and maintaining undistracted mindfulness."
In this way, the evil karma of a bodhisattva from previous lives— such as receiving an unattractive physical body or suffering from many illnesses in future lives,
or being detested by others— is immediately extinguished.
They are born into low-caste families, or into impoverished families, or into frontier regions and families with wrong views;
they encounter evil friends and find no like-minded companions;
and people do not respect them.
Abounding in many sorrows and afflictions;
being incensed by the king;
encountering the ruin of the nation;
The village is dispersed;
kinsmen are estranged;
and friends are surpassed.
One does not encounter Dharma assemblies;
people do not bestow gifts upon one’s needs and desires;
and even if something is obtained, the multitude does not gather in joy.
Or they may receive meager offerings;
they are discarded by the wealthy yet held in affection and respect by the poor;
and though they wish to cultivate wholesome deeds, they encounter many obstacles.
Stubborn ignorance and distraction prevent one from attaining the sequential order of the Dharma;
one lacks servants and attendants;
and whenever one sleeps, one has nightmares or other such dreams, yet these karmic offenses are immediately eliminated.

Bound by past karma and obscured by Māra, they grasp at false signs and allow Māra to gain the advantage; failing to understand all dharmas, they develop a sense of inferiority when confronted with those who receive offerings.
When people are upright and handsome, they consider themselves ugly and feel unloved;
seeing others obtain profit, they give rise to hatred and jealousy, and further disparage one another.
Thus it has been briefly explained. Maitreya!

If there are bodhisattvas who have together cultivated merit under a hundred buddhas and do not wish to let it go to waste, yet because of these causes and conditions they mutually destroy one another—how much more so for those who have not performed such deeds!
Thus it is, Maitreya!

You should be firm in diligence, maintain right mindfulness, and give rise to the power of great patience; having accomplished profound dharmas and the skillful means of wondrous wisdom, those who wish to uphold this Dharma in future ages should arouse diligence.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, and Pramuditarāja Bodhisattva—these sixty bodhisattvas as their leaders—addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
“Having now heard these merits of protecting the Dharma, I shall protect and uphold this sutra in future ages.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“With few desires, free from defilement, and without crookedness or flattery, Always maintaining right mindfulness, one practices the way of detachment.”
With profound patience, firm and unshakable, they protect the precious treasures of the ten directions.
Their deportment is serene and silent, free from defilement; they seek nothing, desire nothing, and remain aloof from dispute.
Their minds are equal to space, leaving no tracks, as their conduct accords with True Suchness and embodies samādhi.
Firmly established in Bodhi ever present before them, Understanding the profound, they are named Perfectly Awakened;
Without regard for hatred or love, remaining unattached, They are thus able to attain this samādhi.
With a mind of equanimity toward enemies and kin, Without discriminatory thoughts regarding Buddhas or virtuous friends,
Cultivating the six points of respectful harmony and maintaining pure precepts— Such a person can swiftly realize this samādhi.
Thoroughly understanding the most supreme in the world, one should discern the billions of marks of the Seals of Dharma;
with wisdom illuminating like the light of the sun, herein is explained the gateway for entering into gnosis.
The sun and moon dwell in the void day and night; likewise, Mount Himavat always abides upon the earth.
So too are Śakra, Brahmā, and the Cakravartin kings, as well as the physician who skillfully heals—all are thus.
This sutra purifies the mind and extinguishes karmic retribution; this sutra subdues demons and is called nectar.
With this divine power and eye, one knows the minds of others, responding appropriately to all various types of beings.
This can remember and know ten billion eons; this can extinguish all craving;
this is the seal of the Tathāgata praised by the Buddhas; this path is as clear as looking at the palm of one's hand.
This sutra compiles and explains the meaning of all emptiness; this is the true dwelling in emptiness and quiescence.
Existence and non-existence are both termed frivolous proliferation; forever relinquishing them without attachment, one upholds the True Dharma.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, some said: "I see that all phenomena are empty like a dream;
all phenomena do not arise and have no agent, yet within them one dwells by establishing the conceptualization of an agent."
Dharmas are empty, unarisen, and without an agent; they are without view, without coming, and without movement.
Whatever dharmas one clings to are called "thieves of the Dharma," yet one says of oneself, "I study emptiness."
If one hears their name or hears the Dharma from them, tears flow in sorrowful weeping and the hair on one's body stands on end;
yet they further praise themselves as non-retrogressive, only to later describe those various evil signs.
Though noble, base, poor, or destitute of wealth and treasure, If I were to obtain the Dharma and gain manifold benefits,
Or if I were to leave the household life and bring glory to my kin, I would give rise to jealousy and malice toward the sons of the Buddha.
Having left the household life for the sake of the unsurpassed path, they desire to practice bodhi yet do not abide in it;
like one who is far from the further shore of the great ocean, they lack correct faith in bodhi.
Dwelling in quietude amidst mountains and marshes, complete in dignified deportment, with pure teachers and friends and a virtuous retinue—
yet seeking out kin and associates for the sake of gain and sustenance, they claim for themselves to be true renunciants.
The renunciant who can accord with this True Dharma, like a lotus flower untainted by attachment,
and practices the sequential stages in accordance with this sutra— this is true bodhi, which is constantly protected.
"O King of Joy, I now instruct you: Be careful not to follow those who learn what is unwholesome;
practice according to the Dharma and be endowed with the virtues of a Buddha—this is how you all should train as I have taught."
Suppose there were fields as vast as ten billion world-systems, and within them were sown seeds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
from each single seed grew fruits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and it was likewise for every single seed that was sown.
Thus, through successive transformations of millions of kinds, they spread and flourish, giving rise to diverse forms;
as numerous as their seeds may be, they cannot be counted, for all of them remain beyond measure.
By these skillful means, throughout the eastern direction, they plant [seeds] in this manner without exception;
so it is in all directions as well, until the Buddhas fill the realms of all these sons.
Each and every Buddha has a hundred heads, and each Buddha head has a hundred tongues;
thus they continue for immeasurable kalpas, all together praising this sutra in accordance with its truth.
The merit of copying, upholding, reading, and reciting, as well as expounding [this teaching], is inexhaustible—
like a single mustard seed compared to Mount Sumeru, or a single blade of grass compared to that which fills all of space.
Like a single drop from the waters of the great ocean, one who should practice this sutra apart from worldly existence,
hearing, receiving, upholding, writing, reading, and reciting it— for this reason I have spoken these verses.
At that time, the Bodhisattva King of Joy, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī the Dharma Prince, and these sixty bodhisattvas who had attained practice without conditions addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"What is meant by 'Dharma,' what constitutes Dharma?
The Buddha told King Nanda:
"That which is called Dharma is without action and without conceptual construction, yet it is expressed through verbal discourse."
“Yes, World-Honored One!
If dharmas are without action and without designation, for what reason are there verbal expressions?
The Buddha said:
“If a dharma is without activity and without designation, it cannot be expressed in such words.

When one thoroughly contemplates all dharmas, they are not obtained, not exhausted, not transcended, not diminished, not extinguished, not craved; they are unarisen, placeless, without location, neither that nor this; they are neither conditioned nor unconditioned, merely nominal or non-nominal, neither mind nor non-mind, neither opposed nor non-opposed, neither associated nor dissociated, equal or non-equal, objective sphere or non-sphere, partial or non-partial, near or non-near, neither defiled nor expressible.”
“Yes, World-Honored One!
How is it that it is neither defiled nor expressible?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! That which is neither defilement nor verbal expression is called nirvāṇa.
At that time, the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If dharmas have such characteristics, what dharma is extinguished?
What dharma can be protected?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“One who gives rise to the conceptualization of dharmas toys with all dharmas;
by toy[ing] with all dharmas, one gives rise to the two extremes of existence and non-existence.”
"To give rise to the two extremes is itself the cessation of dharmas.
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there is no dharma and no cessation of dharmas, nor is there any dispute.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Some may speak of reality as non-different, while others may speak of difference as impermanence;
if one grasps at dharmas by adhering to these two extremes, this is called being inconsistent with the cessation of conceptual proliferation."
The Dharma is without action and without destruction; fundamentally it is not seen in self nor seen in others, nor is there any application of conceptual designations or mindfulness.
To bind mindfulness to emptiness is non-applicability; this Dharma does not arise from false deliberation.
All deliberate activities are the net of Māra.

To have thoughts and calculations is to be called an ordinary person; though all phenomena are fundamentally non-existent, they are falsely grasped, and one deliberates upon phenomena by means of conceptual speech and sound.
Seeking wisdom with wisdom, one does not find wisdom; wisdom ultimately does not arise from wisdom.
To expound the provisional characteristics of conditioned phenomena is neither the possession of wisdom nor the absence of wisdom.
If even a small portion of phenomena were substantially existent, their destruction would constitute the doctrine of annihilationism;
if any phenomenon were to exist as a real abiding entity, then all phenomena would be eternally permanent.
That a fool might relinquish them and then obtain them again would thus result in the disintegration of the aggregates and a violation of the characteristics of phenomena.
Those who are attached to a self and grasp at a real self, yet whose wise minds know that phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent, perceive no duality between clarity and ignorance;
if they hear this teaching being proclaimed, they will be struck with alarm and doubt.
This is to bind one’s mindfulness to the characteristics of extreme views; to speak of nirvāṇa while conditioned things are decaying;
for the mind cannot know the true nature of the mind, nor does the true nature know the mind.
All phenomena are like dreams, yet some speak of "reality" while remaining attached to the view of self.
Phenomena arising from conditions are not the ultimate truth; if phenomena were to cease and be extinguished, they too would not be the truth.
It is through this skillful means that one attains the reality: if the phenomena that arise were truly real, the Buddha himself would have arisen [from them].
The wisdom of the Tathāgata is unattainable; though he teaches all dharmas, there is nothing to be displayed;
though he treats the ailments of the multitude, there is no liberation—this is called the excellent understanding of quiescence.
If nirvāṇa possessed parts, then Buddhas and śrāvakas would have to go there;
yet walls and other such phenomena lack nirvāṇa, so the wise should not give rise to conceptual proliferation.
No one can perceive a real sentient being, nor is there anything that can be pointed out or described as existing;
it is the sentient being themselves who give rise to the appearance of visibility—this is nirvana, free from all attachment.
Some say the aggregates (*skandha*) are the ultimate truth; some say that the cessation of craving is called the Path;
some speak of a single ultimate truth that is neither born nor extinguished; and others further expound upon the Four Noble Truths.
When one seeks, not even a single dharma can be found as a foundation; how much less could one sit beneath the Bodhi tree and perceive the Four Truths?
Those with various defiled minds have gone forth together, only to further corrupt my Dharma by giving rise to false fabrications.
For the sake of the fruits of asceticism and for renown, do not associate with evil friends but stay close to virtuous ones;
like a rhinoceros dwelling alone in the wilderness, remain in accord with the meaning of this samādhi.
Eight billion Buddhas, the Honored Ones among two-legged beings, protectively mind those who write and uphold this sutra;
the devas who have seen the Truth likewise protectively mind them, guarding and shielding them day and night without ever abandoning them.
Immeasurable light shines without end; The brilliance of wisdom guides and reveals a hundred dharma-gates.
Awakening within dreams, one brings them to fulfillment; To uphold this samādhi is truly rare.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī:

“If one wishes to accomplish the Bodhi of a Buddha, one should study this samādhi with single-minded devotion. One shall accomplish the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, great loving-kindness and great compassion; one shall accomplish the Buddha-eye, realize Bodhi for oneself, establish the assembly of śrāvakas, establish the assembly of bodhisattvas, purify the Buddha-land, and achieve the dharāṇī of great wisdom.”

Those who wish to understand the languages of all sentient beings, who wish to attain responsive eloquence, who wish to attain definitive eloquence, who wish to attain the supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*), who wish to preach the non-retrogressive Dharma, who wish to understand all corresponding dharmas, and who wish to clearly comprehend all phenomena, should practice this samādhi.

Why is this? Because when a bodhisattva is in union with this samādhi, they attain the aforementioned merits and are called a Buddha, called one who has studied universally, called an island, called a savior, called one worthy of offerings, called the Omniscient One, called the Tamer, called the Knower of the World, called the Unsurpassed Being, and called the Tathāgata.
To act according to what one has taught, being peerless and equal to the unequaled—this is called the foremost discourse, the discourse on reality, and is supreme.
Why is this so? Mañjuśrī!
"Abiding in this samādhi, I saw the Buddha Dīpaṃkara and immediately attained bodhi.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying,
"So it is, World-Honored One!"

"If, World-Honored One, you attained bodhi immediately upon seeing Dīpaṃkara Buddha, for what reason did you remain within saṃsāra for incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, practicing difficult and painful austerities?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"I perform the work of a Buddha for the sake of sentient beings; I transform sentient beings, causing them to abide in the Three Vehicles, and for their sake I proclaim my original vow."
"Mañjuśrī! At that time, I also attained bodhi and also entered nirvāṇa.
At that moment, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"One who can be in accord with this realizes for themselves immeasurable merit;
the billions of Buddhas of the ten directions all protect and mind such a person.
They shall not regress from the nectar of immortality and shall inconceivably manifest the hundred marks."
Through cultivation, one will certainly obtain the inexhaustible King of Dharanis.
This wisdom-samādhi concentration understands all speech and sounds;
it can destroy the marks of all phenomena and brings liberation by extinguishing all fetters.
Tranquil and well-stilled, neither arising nor ceasing, Unattached, he dispels all doubts;
He accomplishes the ten powers and the marks of excellence, The meritorious virtues of all Buddhas.
With sublime stillness, he understands all sounds, The various and diverse voices of different species.
Gradually explaining [the Dharma] to bring joy, purifying the two extremes of existence and non-existence;
with supreme, decisive wisdom, one eradicates all fetters.
If one can study this sutra, one will decisively realize the Path without doubt.
If, for twenty-one days, one studies this sutra with single-minded devotion,
without indolence or sleep, without following the pleasures of kin and loved ones,
speaking words that are gentle and harmonious, and possessing compassion free from envy—
Cultivating the six points of respectful harmony, one maintains the precepts and attains samādhi.
With an impartial mind and perfect deportment, with a straightforward mind one delights in liberation.
Not constructing dependent origination, one is content and remains unstained by defilements.
Firm and not fickle, manifesting no signs of deceit or falsehood,
like a bird without attachment, one will surely obtain the King of Dhāraṇīs.
The three-thousandfold world system trembles, and the heavens play manifold musical sounds.
They rained down exquisite fragrant flowers, along with hundreds of thousands of banners and canopies;
they also rained down exquisite celestial crowns, conch-shell necklaces and precious pendants,
mani-jewels and pearls, as well as round gems, radiant garments, and robes that bring joy.
In the immeasurable heavens above, the various nāgas and garuḍas,
the nāga kings and asura kings, the bhikṣus and upāsakas,
the bhikṣuṇīs and upāsikās— each stripped off their upper garments.
Pūrṇabhadra scattered jewels over the Buddha, Vowing to seek the unsurpassed path.
I say that this is immeasurable And cannot be fully displayed;
Yet if one gives rise to the bodhicitta, One immediately attains non-retrogression.
"Those who have been tamed and attained arhatship are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
the sentient beings of a hundred worlds, having heard the Dharma, have attained joy.
At that time, when the World-Honored One spoke this Dharma, incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings all resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta.
Eighty nayutas of devas and humans all attained non-retrogression from the unsurpassed path;
sixty-three billion devas and humans attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas;
and countless sentient beings attained arhatship.
In this way, all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who had gathered from the ten directions attained this samādhi.

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the Bodhisattva King of Joy (Ratnarāja) and Mañjuśrī were the leaders, as were these sixty inconceivable bodhisattvas and all the bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa, with Maitreya as their leader.

The noble Kāñcanaprabha, as well as the bodhisattvas gathered from the ten directions, the great śrāvakas, and the fourfold assembly—gods, humans, gandharvas, and asuras—all the worlds, having heard what the Buddha taught, were filled with great joy.
